title: LIMITS — Infinite Limits, Indeterminate Forms & Evaluation of Limits (Step-by-Step)
notes: 📘 TOPIC OUTLINE: Infinite Limits | Indeterminate Forms | Evaluation of Limits (∞/∞ form) | Evaluation of Limits containing Radicals (Rationalization) | Direct Substitution & Simplification Method

♾️ INFINITE LIMIT — CONCEPT: As x approaches a value very close to a point where the denominator approaches 0, the value of the function grows without bound.

Note: 1/0 is UNDEFINED, but 1/(a very small positive number) → a very LARGE positive number, and 1/(a very small negative number) → a very LARGE negative number.
RULE 1: lim(x→0⁺) 1/x = +∞  → As x approaches 0 from the RIGHT (positive side), 1/x grows without bound towards +∞.
RULE 2: lim(x→0⁻) 1/x = −∞  → As x approaches 0 from the LEFT (negative side), 1/x decreases without bound towards −∞.
RULE 3: lim(x→∞) 1/x = 0  → As x grows infinitely large, 1/x shrinks towards 0.

❓ INDETERMINATE FORMS — DEFINITION: These are forms which, upon direct substitution, do NOT determine a unique value of the limit — further simplification (factoring, rationalization, or algebraic manipulation) is required to find the true limiting value.

Simply plugging in the value gives an undefined/ambiguous result, so we must find an equivalent expression that IS defined at that point.

💡 KEY INSIGHT: Whenever a limit reduces to one of these 7 forms after direct substitution, we CANNOT conclude the limit directly — we must simplify using factorization, rationalization (multiplying by conjugate), or dividing every term by the highest power of x, before substituting again.
═══════════ SECTION A: EVALUATION OF LIMITS — DIRECT SUBSTITUTION & SIMPLIFICATION METHOD ═══════════

📐 METHOD 1 — Direct Substitution: If substituting x = a directly into the function gives a DEFINED (finite) value, that value itself IS the limit.

No further work needed.

📐 METHOD 2 — Simplification & Substitution Method: If direct substitution gives an INDETERMINATE form (usually 0/0), factor the numerator and denominator, CANCEL the common factor causing the zero, then substitute again.
Step 1: Try direct substitution → (2²−4)/(2−2) = 0/0 → INDETERMINATE, so we must simplify.
Step 2: Factor the numerator using difference of squares: x²−4 = (x−2)(x+2)
Step 4: Cancel the common factor (x−2): lim(x→2) (x+2)
Step 1: Direct substitution → (4−8+4)/(4−4+10) = 0/10 = 0 → this is DEFINED, so no factoring needed here.
📝 EXAMPLE A4 (Factoring a repeated & simple root together): Evaluate lim(x→2) (x²−4x+4)/(x²−5x+6)  [i.e., (x−2)²/(x−2)(x−3)]
Step 2: Factor numerator: x²−4x+4 = (x−2)(x−2). Factor denominator: x²−5x+6 = (x−2)(x−3)
═══════════ SECTION B: EVALUATION OF LIMITS AT INFINITY (∞/∞ FORM) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: When x → ∞ and BOTH numerator and denominator are polynomials that grow without bound (giving the indeterminate form ∞/∞), DIVIDE every single term of the numerator AND denominator by the HIGHEST power of x present in the expression.

Then apply the rule lim(x→∞) (1/xⁿ) = 0 for any positive power n.
Step 1: Highest power of x in this expression is x². Divide EVERY term (numerator & denominator) by x².
Step 1: Highest power = x². Divide every term by x².
Step 3: As x→∞, all fractional terms with x in the denominator → 0.
Step 1: Highest power = x³. Divide every term by x³.
Step 3: As x→∞, all terms with x in denominator → 0.

💡 GENERAL RULE FOR THIS TYPE (Shortcut): For lim(x→∞) (polynomial of degree m)/(polynomial of degree n): if m = n, the answer is the ratio of the LEADING coefficients; if m < n, the answer is 0; if m > n, the answer is ∞ (limit does not exist as a finite number).
═══════════ SECTION C: EVALUATION OF LIMITS INVOLVING RADICALS (RATIONALIZATION METHOD) ═══════════

📐 METHOD: When the limit expression involves square roots and direct substitution gives 0/0 or ∞−∞, MULTIPLY the numerator and denominator by the CONJUGATE of the radical expression (this uses the identity (√A−√B)(√A+√B) = A−B), which eliminates the square roots from the numerator, allowing cancellation.
Step 1: Direct substitution gives the indeterminate form ∞ − ∞. Multiply and divide by the conjugate √(2x+1) + √(2x).
Step 5: As x→∞, the denominator √(2x+1)+√(2x) grows without bound (→∞), so the whole fraction 1/(large number) → 0
Step 1: Direct substitution gives 0/0 → INDETERMINATE. Multiply numerator and denominator by conjugate (√x + √a).
Step 3: Numerator becomes (x − a) using difference of squares: (√x)²−(√a)² = x − a
Step 5: Cancel the common factor (x−a): lim(x→a) 1/(√x+√a)
📝 EXAMPLE C3: Evaluate lim(x→a) [√(2x) − √(9x−a)]/(√x − √a)   [type seen in notebook — general pattern]
Step 1: Multiply numerator's conjugate AND denominator's conjugate to rationalize BOTH parts, since both involve radicals.
Step 2: Multiply top and bottom by (√(2x)+√(9x−a)) to clear numerator, and by (√x+√a) to clear denominator (apply one after another).
Step 3: After rationalizing the denominator: multiply by (√x+√a)/(√x+√a) → denominator becomes (x−a).
Step 4: Simplify the resulting rational expression, factor out (x−a) from the simplified numerator, and cancel with denominator (x−a).
Step 5: Substitute x = a into the fully-cancelled expression to get the final numeric answer in terms of a.

💡 NOTE: This is a two-stage rationalization problem — rationalize whichever side (numerator or denominator) contains the 0/0-causing radical FIRST, cancel, then handle the remaining radical if needed.
📝 EXAMPLE C4: Evaluate lim(x→64) (⁶√x − 2)/(³√x − 4)   [6th root and cube root example]
Step 2: Let t = ⁶√x, so x = t⁶. Then ³√x = t² (since ³√(t⁶) = t²). As x→64, t→⁶√64 = 2.
📝 EXAMPLE C5: Evaluate lim(x→1) (¹⁰√x − 1)/(⁵√x − 1)   [10th root and 5th root example]
Step 2: Let t = ¹⁰√x, so x = t¹⁰. Then ⁵√x = t² (since ⁵√(t¹⁰) = t²). As x→1, t→1.
═══════════ SECTION D: LIMITS INVOLVING NESTED RADICALS AT INFINITY ═══════════
📝 EXAMPLE D1: Evaluate lim(x→∞) [√(3x+a) − √(2x)] × [√(3x+a)+√(2x)]/[√(3x+a)+√(2x)] type rationalization
Step 1: Multiply and divide by the conjugate to remove the difference of square roots in the numerator.
Step 2: Numerator becomes (3x+a) − 2x = x + a after applying difference of squares.
Step 4: Divide every term (numerator and denominator) by √x (or x, depending on degree matching) to evaluate the ∞/∞ form.
Step 5: Numerator/√x → √x (still grows), denominator/√x → √(3+a/x)+√2 → √3+√2 (finite) as x→∞.

Step 6: Since the numerator still grows unboundedly while denominator approaches a finite constant, the overall limit → ∞ (does not converge to a finite value) UNLESS the original numerator power was matched — always double check degree of numerator vs denominator after rationalizing.

💡 TIP: After rationalizing radicals, ALWAYS re-check whether the resulting expression is now in ∞/∞ or a finite-form — this decides whether you divide by the highest power of x again (Section B method) or simply substitute.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE TO AVOID: Do NOT cancel terms inside a square root directly (e.g., you cannot cancel an 'x' that is buried inside √(2x+a) with an 'x' outside the root) — always rationalize FIRST using the conjugate before attempting any cancellation.

🎯 QUICK SUMMARY OF ALL METHODS: (1) If direct substitution gives a defined value → that IS the answer.

(2) If it gives 0/0 with polynomials → FACTOR and cancel.

(3) If it gives 0/0 with radicals → RATIONALIZE using the conjugate and cancel.

(4) If x→∞ and both parts are polynomials (∞/∞ form) → DIVIDE every term by the highest power of x.

(5) If x→∞ with a difference of radicals (∞−∞ form) → RATIONALIZE using the conjugate first to convert it into a ∞/∞ or finite form, THEN apply method (4) if needed.
